implementation_notes: The JDK's I/O library is the canonical decorator: FilterInputStream 'wraps some other input stream, which it uses as its basic source of data, possibly transforming the data along the way', and its subclasses add one capability each - BufferedInputStream, DataInputStream, PushbackInputStream, GZIPInputStream - with the parallel Reader/Writer hierarchies. Composition happens at construction: new DataInputStream(new GZIPInputStream(new FileInputStream(f))) leaves the caller holding an InputStream, and clients need no knowledge of the layers. It remains the right form whenever the decorated contract has several methods and clients must see the component type; for single-method contracts the functional variant is far less code.

variants.name: java.io filter stream chain (FilterInputStream family)
variants.idiom_name: subclass FilterInputStream/FilterOutputStream (or FilterReader/FilterWriter) and take the wrapped stream in the constructor
variants.implementation_notes: The JDK's I/O library is the canonical decorator: FilterInputStream 'wraps some other input stream, which it uses as its basic source of data, possibly transforming the data along the way', and its subclasses add one capability each - BufferedInputStream, DataInputStream, PushbackInputStream, GZIPInputStream - with the parallel Reader/Writer hierarchies. Composition happens at construction: new DataInputStream(new GZIPInputStream(new FileInputStream(f))) leaves the caller holding an InputStream, and clients need no knowledge of the layers. It remains the right form whenever the decorated contract has several methods and clients must see the component type; for single-method contracts the functional variant is far less code.
variants.code_sketch:
InputStream in = new DataInputStream(              // format layer
        new BufferedInputStream(                       // buffering layer
            new GZIPInputStream(                       // decompression layer
                new FileInputStream("data.gz"))));     // component
int magic = in.readInt();                              // callers still see InputStream
pitfalls: The chain is verbose and its static type is only the outermost wrapper: the FileInputStream underneath cannot be reached without reflection, and adding a layer means editing every construction site.
Identity and type checks break: `instanceof`, casts and libraries that branch on the concrete stream type see the outermost decorator, not the component.
Closing semantics are a contract of the hierarchy - decorators must close the wrapped stream - and custom implementations that forget it leak descriptors even though callers did everything right.

variants.name: Function/UnaryOperator composition with andThen / compose
variants.idiom_name: java.util.function.Function<T,R> and UnaryOperator<T> composed with andThen/compose; lambdas and method references as decorators
variants.implementation_notes: When the component is effectively one operation, the class-per-decorator structure collapses into function composition: Function.andThen returns a composed function that applies this function first and the given function afterwards, so lambdas and method references chain responsibilities - dampen.andThen(triple).andThen(augment) - with no wrapper classes, no interfaces and no allocations beyond the composed function object. This is the modern default for transformation pipelines; keep the java.io-style classes when the decorated contract has several methods (threading every method through functions is the alternative cost) or when checked exceptions, resource lifecycle and per-instance state must be carried by the decorator.
pitfalls: andThen applies the receiver first and then the argument while compose does the opposite; mixing them up silently reverses the pipeline with no type error to catch it.

Function composition has nowhere to put per-instance state or lifecycle: counters, caches, buffers or close/flush semantics still require a wrapper object (or a stateful lambda, which is a race in concurrent use).
Checked exceptions do not fit the functional interfaces - an I/O contract that throws IOException forces back to the classic child classes or to wrapping in unchecked exceptions.
